## Introduction

Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) are equations that involve an unknown 
function of several variables and their partial derivatives.  PDEs are used 
to formulate many applied problems in physics, engineering and optimization 
including head transfer, wave propogation, fluid flow and elasticity.  In this 
series of notes we will cover the fundamentals of PDEs including their 
classification, solution methods and applications.

The study of PDEs is quite complicated and draws on many areas of matHhematics. 
It is recommended to have studied the following topics before tackling PDEs:

* Multivariate Calculus
* Ordinary Differential Equations
* Multidimensional Integration

Some additional topics that are helpful but not strictly necessary include:

* Measure Theory
* Functional Analysis

In making these study notes I have used the following resources:

1. Bright Side of Mathematics: Partial Differential Equations Series.
2. Lecture Notes by Prof. Viktor Grigoryan, Fall 2010, UC Santa Barbara.
3. Lecture Notes by Prof. Denis Labutin, Fall 2026, UC Santa Barbara.

## Partial Derivatives

First recall the following definition of a partial derivative from 
our study of multivariate calculus.

:::{.definition data-title="Partial Derivative"}

A **partial derivative** of a function $u:\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ 
in variables $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ with repect to $j$-th variable 
is the derivative of $u$ with respect to $x_j$ while keeping all other 
variables fixed

$$
\partial_j u = \frac{\partial u}{\partial x_j}, \quad j = 1, 2, \ldots, n,
$$

also written as $D_j u$, $\partial_{x_{j}}$ or $u_{x_j}$.  

:::

Here we have referenced the differential operator $D^n_j$ to denote the
$n$-th partial derivative with respect to the $j$-th variable.  

:::{.definition data-title="Multi-Index"}

A **multi-index** $\alpha = (\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n)$ is an $n$-tuple of
non-negative integers.  The **order** of a multi-index is given by 
$\| \alpha \| = \alpha_1 + \ldots  + \alpha_n$.  We define

$$
D^\alpha
  = \partial_1^{\alpha_1} \ldots \partial_n^{\alpha_n} 
  = \frac{\partial^{\| \alpha \|}}{\partial x_1^{\alpha_1} \ldots \partial x_n^{\alpha_n}}
$$

:::

:::{.example}

Consider the function $u(x,y) = 2x^2 + 4y^3 + 2xy$.  The partial derivative of 
$f$ with respect to $x$ and $y$ respectively are given by

$$
u_x = 4x + 2y, \quad u_y = 12y^2 + 2x.
$$

:::

## Partial Differential Equations

:::{.definition data-title="Partial Differential Equation"}

A **partial differential equation (PDE)** is an equation of an unknown 
function $u:\Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ (where typically 
$\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ open, $n \ge 2$) involving some 
partial derivative of $u$ 

$$
F(x, u(x), (D^\alpha u)(x)) = 0,
$$

where $F$ is a given function, $\alpha$ is a multi-index, and $D^\alpha u$ 
denotes the partial derivative of $u$ corresponding to the multi-index 
$\alpha$.

:::

A function $u:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$ is a **(classical)** solution of a PDE if 
all partial derivatives appearing in the PDE are well-defined 
and the function $u$ satisfies the PDE at all points in $\Omega$. 

:::{.example}

A simple example of a PDE for function $u(x,y)$ written in different notations

$$
\begin{align*}
\cos (u) + 3u_{x} + 2u\cdot u_{xy} & = 0 \\
\cos (u) + 3 \partial_ x u + 2 u\cdot \partial _{xy} u & = 0\\
\cos (u) + 3Dx + 2u\cdot D_x D_y u & = 0.
\end{align*}
$$

:::

:::{.definition data-title="Order of a PDE"}

The **order** of a PDE is the order of the highest partial derivative in 
the equation.  

:::

:::{.example}
The order of our last example is 2 since the highest order partial derivative 
is $u_{xy}$.
:::

## Classification of PDEs

There are two lenses through which to view PDEs: the mathematical structure
and the physical phenomena they model.  

### Classification by Mathematical Structure

Let's first consider mathematical structure of a PDEs up to second order. 
We write the principal part (the highest-order terms) as

$$
Lu = \sum_{i,j=1}^{n} a_{ij}(x) u_{x_i x_j} + (\text{lower order terms}), 
\quad A = (a_{ij})_{i,j=1}^{n}~ \text{(symmetric)}.
$$

The type depends on the eigenvalues of $A$:

1. Elliptic PDEs - all eigenvalues of $A$ are non-zero and have the same sign.
2. Parabolic PDEs - one eigenvalue of $A$ is zero and the rest have the same sign.
3. Hyperbolic PDEs - one eigenvalue of $A$ has a different sign than the rest.

In two dimensions, the classification can be determined by the discriminant of the
principal part of the PDE.  For a second-order PDE in two variables $x$ and
$y$ of the form

$$
a u_{xx} + b u_{xy} + c u_{yy} + (\ \text{lower order terms}) = 0, 
$$
the PDE is classified as follows:

$$
\begin{cases}
b^2 - 4ac < 0 & \text{elliptic} \\
b^2 - 4ac = 0 & \text{parabolic} \\
b^2 - 4ac > 0 & \text{hyperbolic}.
\end{cases}
$$

The prototypical examples of each type of PDE are given in Table 1 below.

| Type | Prototypical Example | Typical Behavior | 
|------|---------------------|-----------------|
| Elliptic | Laplace's Equation: $\Delta u = 0$, Poisson's Equation: $-\Delta u = f$.  | Equilibrium or steady state, boundary value problems, smooth solutions, every point influences each other.  |
| Parabolic | Heat Equation: $u_t = \Delta u$ | Smoothing, irreversible in time, infinite propogation speed, initial-boundary value problems. |
| Hyperbolic | Wave Equation: $u_{tt}=c^2\Delta u$ | Finite propogation speed, real characteristics, singularities travel, time-reversible. |

### Classification by Physical Phenomena

Alternatively, PDEs can be classified by asking what a solution does as 
time evolves.  A good way to see the distinction is to test each equation on a
plane wave $u=\exp (i(kx - \omega  t)$, which gives a dispersion relation 
$\omega  = \omega (k)$.

| Phenomenon | Model Equation | Dispersion Relation | Observations |
|------------|----------------|--------------------|--------------|
| Transport (Advection) | $u_t + c u_x = 0$ | $\omega = ck$ | Profile moves rigidly at speed $c$: $u = f(x-ct)$. |
| Diffusion | $u_t = D u_{xx}$ | $\omega = -iDk^2$ | Modes decay like $\exp(-iDk^2)$, so high frequencies die fastest and the profile smooths and spreads. |
| Wave Propogation | $u_{tt} = c^2 u_{xx}$ | $\omega = \pm ck$ | Two transport waves, profile moves rigidly at speed $c$: $u = f(x-ct) + g(x+ct)$. |
| Dispersion (Schroedinger) | $i u_t = -\frac{1}{2} u_{xx}$ | $\omega = \frac{1}{2} k^2$ | Modes rotate in the complex plane at different speeds, so the profile spreads and oscillates. |


## Linear PDEs

:::{.definition data-title="Linear PDE"}

The general form of a **linear PDE** of order $m$ is given by

$$
\sum_{|\alpha| \le m} a_\alpha(x) (D^\alpha u)(x) = f(x), \quad x \in \Omega,
$$

where $a_\alpha$ and $f$ are given functions, $\alpha$ is a multi-index, and
$D^\alpha u$ denotes the partial derivative of $u$ corresponding to the
multi-index $\alpha$.

:::

:::{.definition data-title="Linear Operator"}

A **linear operator** $L$ is a mapping from a vector space $V$ to itself
that satisfies the following properties for all $u, v \in V$ and scalars $c$:

$$
L(cu+v) = cL(u) + L(v).
$$

:::
